working_narrative: Care organizations cannot reliably add appointments, beds, shifts, or services because recruitment, retention, and pipeline capacity are limiting delivery.
cross_contexts: hospital; behavioral health; FQHC; rural; home health; hospice; SNF; nursing
why_it_recurs: The same capacity language appears across operator, workforce, policy, and creator channels, but each setting names a different labor bottleneck.
implication_for_mindfultext: Start with a setting-specific workforce/work-design hypothesis; avoid a generic burnout product narrative.

working_narrative: Turnover, burnout, emotional load, safety, and weak work design reduce the reliable capacity of already-thin teams.
cross_contexts: hospital; behavioral health; FQHC; post-acute; nursing
why_it_recurs: The field increasingly links worker experience to throughput, quality, continuity, and cost rather than treating wellness as a standalone benefit.
implication_for_mindfultext: Test whether care leaders describe the problem as retention, safety, workload, moral injury, or workflow before selecting language.

working_narrative: Thin margins, reimbursement pressure, grant uncertainty, Medicaid exposure, and rising labor costs turn staffing and service availability into financial-continuity problems.
cross_contexts: FQHC; rural; hospital; hospice; home health; behavioral health
why_it_recurs: Funding is repeatedly discussed as the condition that allows organizations to recruit, retain, expand, and preserve services.
implication_for_mindfultext: Pair workforce discovery with budget and reimbursement context; do not infer willingness to pay from need.

working_narrative: Prior authorization, denials, documentation, compliance, and reporting consume scarce clinical and operational time and delay care.
cross_contexts: hospital; primary care; behavioral health; FQHC; physician practice
why_it_recurs: Recent material makes administrative burden measurable and connects it to burnout and patient delay; historical material shows it is persistent, not new.
implication_for_mindfultext: Treat workflow burden as a concrete discovery target; ask which task, role, and handoff is costly.

working_narrative: Waits, limited appointments, service reductions, hospital and maternity closures, and discharge bottlenecks are public symptoms of constrained delivery capacity.
cross_contexts: rural; FQHC; behavioral health; hospital; SNF; home care
why_it_recurs: Access is the patient-facing language that translates staffing, finance, geography, and coordination problems into visible consequences.
implication_for_mindfultext: Use access outcomes as the bridge between internal workforce pain and mission-level urgency.

working_narrative: CCBHCs, integrated behavioral health, care transitions, home-based care, community health workers, and social services are framed as responses to fragmented delivery.
cross_contexts: behavioral health; FQHC; hospital; home health; rural
why_it_recurs: Complex patients and crisis demand expose handoff failures; field narratives increasingly emphasize coordinated, team-based, community delivery.
implication_for_mindfultext: Narrow to one high-friction handoff or role rather than claiming to fix coordination broadly.

working_narrative: Behavioral-health organizations are expected to provide low-barrier access, crisis response, integrated services, and continuity despite workforce and payment constraints.
why_it_recurs: CCBHC expansion and crisis-system conversations make access, coordination, and workforce capacity inseparable.
implication_for_mindfultext: SEG-002 is the strongest next branch for a care-team/workflow hypothesis, but CCBHC requirements create substantial operational load.

short_name: Rural delivery is a fragile local system
working_narrative: Geography, closures, broadband, transport, training pipelines, and low service volume compound workforce and finance problems in rural communities.
why_it_recurs: Rural sources describe a reinforcing loop: service loss drives travel and workforce loss, which further weakens service viability.
implication_for_mindfultext: A rural hypothesis must name the local role, service, and infrastructure constraint; national messaging is too coarse.

short_name: Technology is a capacity lever with conditions
working_narrative: AI documentation, telehealth, interoperability, scheduling, and decision support are presented as ways to extend capacity, but adoption, governance, trust, and workflow fit remain unresolved.
cross_contexts: hospital; FQHC; behavioral health; rural; home care
why_it_recurs: Technology is now a dominant proposed response, but field sources repeatedly qualify it with implementation and accountability concerns.
implication_for_mindfultext: Research the task-level workflow and adoption burden before treating AI as a solution or category.

working_narrative: Minimum staffing, safety, fraud oversight, quality reporting, and payer controls seek accountability but can collide with recruitability and operating reality.
cross_contexts: SNF; hospice; home health; hospital; behavioral health
why_it_recurs: Recent regulation makes the tension visible: stakeholders agree on quality goals but disagree on feasible standards and who bears the cost.
implication_for_mindfultext: Map the tradeoff between compliance work and care capacity; avoid efficacy claims without outcome evidence.
